stories.headline: Ravens' Humphrey expresses displeasure over 'slander' against QB Jackson
stories.summary: Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey voiced his displeasure over what he called "slander" against quarterback Lamar Jackson.
stories.body:
OWINGS MILLS, Md. -- Baltimore Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey voiced his displeasure over what he called "slander" against quarterback Lamar Jackson.

On Thursday, Humphrey went on a tangent after being asked how Jackson looked at practice. Jackson returned to the field this week after missing the last two games with a left ankle injury.

"It seems like Lamar's the only quarterback kind of gets the slander that he gets for anytime anything is going on," Humphrey said. "I feel like you just don't see these same articles. I'm in the hot tub and it's this, that and the third. Unfair treatment."

Humphrey was asked if he was referring to "injury" slander and he didn't clarify.

Humphrey then said, "I just feel like sometimes it seems like it gets away from ... I don't know if it's because of lack of agent or what, that no one can kind of defend him. But I do know this, if Lamar Jackson can play, if he's healthy enough to play, he will play and that's kind of all I can say for that."

When asked again exactly what he meant, Humphrey replied, "Whatever I said is whatever I said. You can take it however you want."

Jackson, who sprained his ankle 18 days ago, moved around well at Thursday's practice. He participated in every drill during the media viewing portion. He was listed as a limited participant for the second straight day.

Before bringing up the "slander" against Jackson, Humphrey was initially asked about how Jackson looked at practice.

"I think anything relating to Lamar is the thing that I don't talk about," Humphrey said. "I think the only one that really does talk about [Lamar] is Lamar. I think if Lamar can play, it'd be great. If he doesn't, we got Snoop [backup Tyler Huntley]."

If Jackson can play Sunday against the Cincinnati Bengals, it would be a timely return. Jackson is 11-2 in his career against the Bengals, throwing 24 touchdowns against six interceptions.

stories.headline: Umpires Nic Lentz, Gabe Morales to make World Series debuts
stories.summary: Nic Lentz and Gabe Morales will make their World Series umpiring debuts, part of a crew headed by James Hoye for the matchup between the Brewers and Rays.
stories.body:
MILWAUKEE -- Nic Lentz and Gabe Morales will make their World Series umpiring debuts, part of a crew headed by James Hoye for the matchup between the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays that starts Friday night.

Dan Bellino, Vic Carapazza, Tripp Gibson and Jim Wolf also will work the World Series. It will be the third World Series for both Hoye and Wolf, and the second each for Bellino, Carapazza and Gibson.

Lentz made his big league debut in 2016 and at 36 will be the youngest Series ump since Pat Hoberg in 2022.

Morales will be the plate umpire for Friday's opener, with Lentz at first, Hoye at second, Carapazza at third, Bellino in left and Gibson in right.

Wolf will work the plate in Game 2 and be followed by Lentz, Hoye, Carapazza, Bellino and Gibson.

Bellino will be the crew chief in Game 3, when Hoye is the reserve.

Lentz had a 48.3% overturn rate in the first season of the ABS ball/strike system of robot umpires, ninth-best among 76 umpires with 100 or more challenges, according to taptochallenge.com. Gibson was 19th at 50.4%, Morales 21st at 50.9%, Carapazza 28th at 52%, Hoye 29th at 52.3%, Wolf 39th at 53.7% and Bellino 65th at 59.9%.

Gibson, Hoye, Lentz and Morales had perfect ABS records in the Division Series, each upheld on two challenges. Teams won 2 of 4 against Bellino and 2 of 5 against Carapazza.

Wolf did not have a plate game in the Division Series.

Hoye, 55, also worked the Series in 2019 and 2022, including the plate for Game 4 of the 2019 matchup between Washington and Houston and the 2022 opener between Philadelphia and Houston.

The 45-year-old Gibson was behind the plate for Game 4 in 2022, only the second no-hitter in World Series history when Houston's Cristian Javier, Bryan Abreu, Rafael Montero and Ryan Pressly combined to pitch in a 5-0 victory.

Wolf, 57, also worked the Series in 2015 and 2019. The 48-year-old Bellino worked the Series in 2021 and the 47-year-old Carapazza in 2023.

Wolf made his major league debut in 1999, Hoye in 2003 and Gibson in 2013. Bellino (48) debuted in 2008, Carapazza (47) in 2010 and Morales (42) in 2014.

Alfonso Márquez and D.J. Reyburn will be the video review umpires at the replay operations center in the commissioner's office in New York.

stories.headline: Transfer rumors, news: Arsenal want £55M in any Gyökeres deal
stories.summary: Arsenal has set their valuation for Viktor Gyökeres' transfer fee if the striker does depart in the next year. Transfer Talk has the latest.
stories.body:
Arsenal want £55 million in any potential deal for striker Viktor Gyökeres. Meanwhile, Manchester United are considering refreshing their back four, with three senior defender's contracts up at the end of the season.

Join us for the latest transfer news and rumors from around the globe.

Transfers home page | Men's summer grades | Women's grades

Trending rumors

- If Viktor Gyökeres does leave Arsenal in the next year, then the North London club has set a valuation of £55 million on a potential exit, reports Football Insider. That is the same amount as the initial fee the Gunners paid Sporting CP to land the striker last summer. However, after a slow start to the current campaign, the Sweden international continues to be linked with a possible move away. Clubs in Italy, Spain, and elsewhere in England are keeping track of the situation, should the 28-year-old become available.

- Harry Maguire, Luke Shaw, and Lisandro Martínez are playing for their futures at Old Trafford, with their contracts due to expire next summer. That's according to according to TEAMtalk, which claims that United are not rushing to make a decision on the three defenders. That comes as preparations are being put in place for potential defensive reinforcements in 2027, with center back and left back set to be the main areas of consideration.

- Chelsea are showing interest in a move for Brighton midfielder Yasin Ayari, claims TEAMtalk. The 23-year-old Sweden international is in talks with the Seagulls over a contract extension, with his deal expiring in the summer, though the club has the option to extend it by a further year. However, while there are hopes of sealing a long-term stay with the club, talks have stalled over an improved contract. That has brought Chelsea into the conversation, with the Blues eyeing another swoop on Brighton, while Turkish Super Lig side Galatasaray are also monitoring the situation.

- Arsenal are among a group of teams following a potential switch for Monza striker Gustavo Varela. That's according to Mundo Deportivo, which claims that the Gunners are joined by Napoli and the 21-year-old's former club, Benfica, in keeping track of his progress. Varela has scored eight goals in seven matches across all competitions for Monza, making an impressive start with his new club. While Benfica is keen on a return, there is no clause that could guarantee a move back to Portugal, though there is a clause that will allow for the club to match an offer accepted from another club. However, with Arsenal and Napoli in the mix, that prospect has been described as difficult.

- Liverpool are in no rush to engage in conversations with Alexis Mac Allister over a new contract, despite the player voicing his disappointment at the lack of an offer earlier this season. That's according to The Telegraph, which claims that the Reds are yet to open talks, as the Argentina international has entered the final two years of his deal at Anfield. The 27-year-old moved to Merseyside from Brighton for £35 million back in 2023, and has featured 161 times for Liverpool since then.

Other rumors
- Manchester United, Arsenal and Newcastle United have all been keeping track of AS Roma defender Wesley, with the 23-year-old Brazilian valued between €50 million and €60 million by the Serie A club. (TEAMtalk)

- Nine clubs are tracking a potential move for Eintracht Frankfurt youngster Niko Ilićević, including the likes of Liverpool, Manchester City, Chelsea and Tottenham from England, alongside Barcelona and Real Madrid in Europe. The attacking midfielder has been monitored heavily by several other clubs. (TEAMtalk)

- Manchester City, Chelsea, Newcastle United, Everton and Leeds United are the latest teams to be tracking Club Brugge striker Nicolò Tresoldi, 22, after attracting attention from plenty of teams with his Champions League displays. (Ekrem Konur)

- Barcelona and Atletico Madrid are among the sides monitoring the future of Lisandro Martínez, with the Manchester United defender now in the final year of his contract. United hold the option of an extra year on his deal. (Ekrem Konur)

- Liverpool are continuing to work on a new contract for Rio Ngumoha, with the club setting a clear stance on no exit for the 18-year-old winger in the coming transfer windows. (Fabrizio Romano)

- Lorenzo Lucca could leave Napoli in the January transfer window, with the 26-year-old striker free to move in the winter. (Nicolò Schira)

- Everton are eyeing a deal for Dinamo Zagreb striker Dion Beljo as one of several options for the forward ranks this January. The 24-year-old has 15 goals in 15 games for his club this season. (Football Insider)

- Gleison Bremer could push to leave Juventus in the January transfer window, with Bayer Leverkusen pushing to land the Brazilian defender. (La Gazzetta dello Sport)

stories.headline: Oliver Bearman 'ready to fight for podiums' with eye on joining top-four team
stories.summary: Oliver Bearman has said he believes he is ready to fight for Formula 1 podiums as the British driver made clear his ambition to drive for a top-four team.
stories.body:
Oliver Bearman has said he believes he is ready to fight for Formula 1 podiums as the British driver made clear his ambition to drive for a top-four team.

The 21-year-old is in his second full season in the sport with Haas but remains a Ferrari academy driver.

Bearman, who made a stunning F1 debut for the Scuderia when he stepped in as a last-minute replacement for Carlos Sainz in Saudi Arabia in 2024, says a deal for him to extend his stay with Haas beyond this season is close to being agreed.

But Bearman, who has scored 23 of Haas' 30 points to sit 13th in the standings, has made no secret of his goal to drive at the top end of the grid.

"I'm committed to Haas. You know, I'm happy to be in F1 but, of course, looking into the medium-long term, I also feel like I'm ready to fight for podiums and fight at the front," Bearman said.

"In terms of a midfield team, Haas is the team that I want to be with and I see my future with. But at some point as well, I feel like I've earned the opportunity to go out and look for a top-four team.

"And of course, with my link with Ferrari, that would be my ultimate goal."

- Kimi Antonelli is on the brink of F1 history -- but first, there's a car to wash and pranks to pull

- British teenager Freddie Slater to make F1 practice debut for Audi in Mexico and Brazil

- Christian Horner to Mercedes? Ex-Red Bull boss reveals pre-Toto Wolff approach

Haas announced last week that Rafael Camara, currently leader of the F2 championship, will join them in 2027.

The 21-year-old Brazilian -- three days older than Bearman -- is also part of the Ferrari academy set-up, with the pair having joined the Scuderia on the same day.

Bearman concedes it could be seen as a shoot-out between them to land a potential Ferrari seat but believes he is ready to step up and lead the team, following the departure of Esteban Ocon.

"We're the same age. Obviously Rafa has less experience than me in Formula 1, but I guess that for Ferrari it's also a good thing to see who they want to put in their car in the medium term," Bearman added.

"Of course, my goal is to put myself in the best position."

stories.headline: How a UConn influence is helping fuel the Valkyries in WNBA Finals
stories.summary: Former Huskies Gabby Williams, Tiffany Hayes, Kiah Stokes and Kaitlyn Chen look to help Golden State even the Finals.
stories.body:
With her teammates huddled around her, Gabby Williams leaned in, seemingly looking at every one of them as she gestured and pointed emphatically. Williams' Golden State Valkyries had just lost for the second straight game, falling behind the Atlanta Dream 2-1 in the WNBA Finals.

Williams sent a message to her teammates. Now it's time for the Valkyries to try to send one to the Dream as they attempt to rally in the best-of-seven series, which continues Saturday (1 p.m. ET) in Game 4 at State Farm Arena in Atlanta.

If they can, the Valkyries will be channeling a large amount of UConn Huskies influence.

Williams is one of four Valkyries -- along with Tiffany Hayes, Kiah Stokes and Kaitlyn Chen -- who won national championships at UConn. Their paths to get here and the roles they have played varied, but they all were influenced by the women's college program that has won the most NCAA titles (12) and sent the most players (54) to the WNBA.

"Every kid that spent that time here has certain qualities that make you win championships," UConn coach Geno Auriemma told reporters in Connecticut earlier this month. "And I don't think I'd be overstating it that if those four were not on that team, they wouldn't be where they are today."

The Golden State franchise and UConn don't have much in common in terms of history. The expansion Valkyries launched last year. Auriemma is entering his 42nd season at UConn. But under coach Natalie Nakase, the Valkyries already have developed an elite defensive commitment that Auriemma's teams always have. Golden State's style worked in beating the Dallas Wings 2-1 in the first round and sweeping the Las Vegas Aces 3-0 in the semifinals.

It also helped them prevail 68-64 in Game 1 of the Finals this past Saturday in San Francisco. But in Games 2 and 3, the Dream have cracked the code, flipping the Valkyries' combined 36 turnovers into 46 points to win 79-65 on Monday in San Francisco and 97-71 on Wednesday in Atlanta.

To even the series, the Valkyries need to make Game 4 on Saturday look more like Game 1. Cutting down on turnovers is the first job, but getting back their swag is important, too. The No. 2 Valkyries are the higher seed, and they knocked off the defending-champion Aces. But Golden State hasn't looked like that team since halftime of Game 2.

Williams' animated postgame callout to her teammates could help reignite the fire.

"I think passion and emotion in sports is huge," Nakase said. "What's really good about our team is we embrace it. We love the fight. We love the screaming."

Even if they don't all show it the same way.

"This is the Finals, is it not emotional?" Stokes said, then added with her trademark deadpan humor, "Not everyone is emotionless like me."

Hayes -- who is more on the passionate side in her playing style and personality -- is the oldest of the "West Coast Huskies." The 37-year-old guard won NCAA titles in 2009 and 2010 with UConn, then in 2012 was drafted by Atlanta. She spent her first 10 seasons with the Dream, then was traded to the Connecticut Sun in 2023.

At the end of that year, she announced her retirement, which didn't last long. She played for Las Vegas in 2024, then joined former Aces assistant Nakase in Golden State the past two seasons.

Hayes is seeking her first WNBA title. To get it, the Valkyries must beat the franchise with which Hayes spent most of her pro career. Her UConn days might be pretty far in the rearview mirror, but she still has Huskies DNA.

"It starts with the type of players they recruit there," Hayes said. "Being able to take constructive criticism and stay a positive person. I was that person when they recruited me, and it's really carried with me from my time there.

"Coach always wanted me to get better, and though that came with some hard times, that's part of growing. I really respect when people are that way with me, because it has really helped me as a player."

Stokes has won three WNBA titles, all with the Aces. She opted to move to Golden State as a free agent this season, as did Williams, who previously was with the Seattle Storm. They were teammates for one season at UConn, 2014-15. Stokes was a senior and Williams a freshman as the Huskies went 38-1, winning the national championship.

Stokes has a more low-key, laid-back personality, but the fire can come out in her on court, especially with her specialty: defense. Stokes averaged 5.8 rebounds and 1.7 blocks in the regular season, numbers that have jumped to 9.6 and 2.6 in the playoffs.

"One thing UConn taught me was to play through adversity when things aren't going your way," Stokes said about an attitude that can help Golden State in this series. "Geno would always make the practices so hard, the games would seem easier."

Williams has led the Valkyries in scoring this season (14.4 PPG in the regular season and 21.2 in the playoffs). But she praises Stokes for doing all the detail-oriented things that don't always get much acclaim yet are crucial to success, such as screening and passing.

She also cites Stokes' mentality, which Williams shares and thinks is the hallmark of UConn's program.

"The biggest thing with UConn culture is putting the team first," Williams said. "Giving up a good shot for a great shot. Putting winning and culture before individual accolades."

As for Chen, she doesn't seem to mind being underestimated. To the contrary, she not only expects it, she has turned it into her superpower.

"She doesn't care if other people don't believe in her," Nakase said. "Kaitlyn wants to be the best."

Chen spent three seasons at Princeton playing for former UConn player Carla Berube, then transferred her senior year to UConn. Chen won the 2025 NCAA title alongside fellow guards Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd, the past two WNBA No. 1 draft picks.

Chen was selected No. 30 in 2025 by the Valkyries, bringing the California native back to her home state. Third-round picks often don't make WNBA rosters, but Chen is in her second season. She has appeared in every game in 2026, averaging 7.2 points in the regular season and 5.7 in the playoffs.

Even though Chen was at UConn just one season, with the influence of Berube's coaching, it almost felt like she was a Huskies-type player all along.

"At UConn, you're playing in such a specific system that really values defense and values ball control on offense," Chen said. "I feel like it's similar to how we do things here.

"Playing in that system, for Coach Auriemma, and also getting to play alongside so many really great players, helped me figure out how to play within my role."

There have been so many UConn players in the WNBA, Auriemma almost always has multiple rooting interests during the playoffs. Another of his former players, Renee Montgomery, is an Atlanta Dream co-owner and executive. But on court, the Valkyries' four former Huskies are carrying the UConn torch to the end of the WNBA season.

"I'm really proud of all of them," Auriemma said, "and that's probably the one team that I've watched play the most."

Stokes said she doesn't necessarily think that often about the UConn connection, since there are great WNBA players from all over. But at times she is reminded there is something tangible to it. Stokes recalled first talking to Nakase about it when both were with the Aces.

"She loves UConn players because they have the mindset, the work ethic," Stokes said. "They understand the game."

Alexa Philippou contributed to this report.

stories.headline: In-the-dark Kane trying not to 'stress' over Monday's Ballon d'Or reveal
stories.summary: Bayern striker Harry Kane said he would prefer to know ahead of time whether he has won the Ballon D'Or, adding he is still in the dark over Monday's decision.
stories.body:
Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane said he would prefer to know ahead of time whether he has won the Ballon D'Or, adding he is still in the dark over Monday's decision.

The 33-year-old is the bookmakers' favourite to become the first Englishman to win the coveted prize since Michael Owen in 2001, but he faces competition from Barcelona's Lamine Yamal and Inter Miami CF's Lionel Messi among others on the 30-man shortlist.

As of 2024, organisers France Football insist they do not warn the winners in advance. That did not stop Real Madrid boycotting the event that year upon learning via a leak that Vinícius Júnior had been overlooked in favour of Rodri.

Kane scored for the tenth consecutive Champions League game on Wednesday as Bayern Munich drew 2-2 with Arsenal at Allianz Arena. Only Cristiano Ronaldo (11) has a longer streak in the competition's history and speaking to reporters after the game, Kane said: "They want everyone to go, all the big names there and there will be more people watching it if they don't know, so I can understand why.

"I think my wife would prefer to know and my family, it's very stressful for everyone. From my point of view, of course, I'd love to know to just kind of see and not have to wait throughout the whole night. But it is their decision, I can't control that. We'll have to just enjoy it and try not to stress out too much.

"I try not to think about it. Obviously it is hard not to. There are always rum ours flying around and you try to stay away from it. We have important games today and I know we have another important one on Sunday before the event on Monday so that's where my focus is.

"Of course I am going to try and enjoy Monday night as much as possible. It is a big occasion so we will have to wait and see."

Bayern have drawn two and won once in the League Phase of the UCL so far, leaving them in 14th place in the table. The Bundesliga champions face third-place Freiburg on Sunday as they try to remain atop of Germany's top flight.

stories.headline: Wysh List: Why NHL fighting is up -- and getting noticed
stories.summary: Through 120 games, there were 34 games with one or more fights, up over the last two seasons (25 and 26).
stories.body:
The boys are fighting.

According to the NHL, there has been an uptick in on-ice fisticuffs this season. Through 120 games, there were 34 games with one or more fights. That's up over last season (25) and the 2024-25 season (26).

"Definitely way more fights," one NHL veteran player told ESPN. "Way more physicality and competitiveness. Which I think is great for the league, because it's something that sets the NHL apart from all the other major sports leagues."

This is true. I'm not sure how many people tuned into NBA opening night to see if LeBron was going to throw hands with Karl-Anthony Towns to make an impression on his new teammates in Philly. The NHL's biggest stars will, however, punch people in the face.

Nathan MacKinnon of the Colorado Avalanche led the NHL with 53 goals last season and was second in ESPN's top 100 player ranking for this season. Last Tuesday, he sat in the Colorado dressing room with stitches across his bloody nose and a throbbing bruise under his left eye after a fight with Dallas Stars center Roope Hintz.

"That was crazy," said Matt Rempe of the New York Rangers, a noted pugilist that was in awe of MacKinnon-Hintz I. "They were both just chucking there, they were both just throwing bombs. Two skilled guys who were throwing, so it was pretty awesome."

It was MacKinnon's second fight of the season, having previously traded blows with Los Angeles Kings defenseman Brandt Clarke.

"The way we all grow up in the Maritimes is pretty gritty, Most guys from that area are feisty. I think it's good to do it sometimes. I might be done for the year, but I guess you never know," MacKinnon said after his second bout. "Getting punched is not that fun. But the guys seemed to like it, so maybe I'll do it a couple more times."

ESPN analyst Erik Johnson played with MacKinnon for 11 seasons and won the Stanley Cup with him in 2022.

"I'm actually surprised he doesn't fight more. He's so intense and he'd be the first to admit he has a screw loose. When that screw wiggles loose, you don't want to be in his path," Johnson said.

As Johnson noted, MacKinnon added Muay Thai to his training regimen, which may be a factor in his recent pugilism. He also thinks Nate's two fights might have created a copycat effect in the NHL this season.

"When you see a guy like MacKinnon do it, maybe that has a trickle-down effect to other players being like, 'Oh, I can do this too,'" he said.

There are a lot of theories why fighting might be on the rise in the NHL this season. One veteran player said that it's a surefire way to instantly create chemistry with teammates.

"When you're on a new team and you're trying to establish yourself with that team, you want to show that you're all-in," he said. "You want to have your teammates appreciate you and standing up for your buddy or for the big hits. I think that's part of it, the camaraderie."

Another player told ESPN that fights help snap some players into a more competitive mindset.

"I know there's a few guys around the league that want to make sure they get a fight in early in the season, just to remind them of the physicality. Sort of an, 'I can still do this,'" the player said. "Nobody wants to fight in preseason, because it's pointless. But in your first early regular-season games, if something happens and there's an opportunity, there's a fight."

About that preseason: Daniel Gallant, who runs HockeyFights.com, believes the league's truncated training camps -- thanks to a move to an 84-game season -- could be an influence.

"I think that opened the door for some players to want to make an impact and impression," he said.

According to HockeyFights, last season saw the most unique players register a fight (288) since the 2013-14 campaign. Gallant's theory is that teams are finding talent to fill their lineup that can skate well and set the tone physically.

"To me, fighting in hockey sits at a bit of a tipping point," he said. "With the aforementioned increase in players willing to drop the gloves, the chance for more exciting fights coming on any given night increases."

Of course, the most frequent fighters don't have the ice time or accolades of a Nathan MacKinnon. Players such as Columbus Blue Jackets forward Mathieu Olivier and Boston Bruins forward Mark Kastelic (tied for the league lead with 10 fights last season) drop the gloves with frequency. Gallant cites Arber Xhekaj (Montreal Canadiens), Scott Sabourin (Tampa Bay Lightning) and Jack McBain (Utah Mammoth) as fighters worth watching.

McBain already had a fight of the year candidate with Edmonton Oilers forward Trent Frederic, with both players absolutely unloading haymakers before leaving for their dressing rooms. Oilers star Connor McDavid could be seen smiling widely as he tapped his stick on the boards in appreciation.

It's worth asking: Is hockey fighting having a moment after years of decline?

Maybe for fans outside of the hockey bubble.

Consider that McBain vs. Frederic was the No. 2 TikTok video across all ESPN accounts last week. Not just hockey -- everything, with the NFL, college football and the MLB playoffs in full swing.

The greatest evidence of this uptick in popularity was back in 2025, when three fights in nine seconds between the USA and Canada launched the 4 Nations Face-Off into becoming a massive success ... while launching the Tkachuk brothers into a successful podcasting side hustle. Of course, it helps that the Tkachuks are both stars and among the best offensive players in the NHL.

It's an interesting dynamic when goal scorers fight. The 2004 Stanley Cup Final is known for two things: Existing on the precipice of the lockout, and having been the series where Calgary's Jarome Iginla and Tampa Bay's Vincent Lecavalier had an unexpected and epic throwdown.

I remember talking to San Jose Sharks players about watching Joe Thornton fight, as he averaged one or two annually for his first dozen seasons. They'd get up on the bench and understand that Jumbo had set the tone.

"I think it surprises you when you see guys that you wouldn't expect to fight end up fighting. That would definitely get you fired up," Johnson said. "Don't get me wrong: You're equally pumped when you have a guy on your team known for fighting that does his job. But I think it gives you a little boost seeing one of your best players do it, for sure."

MacKinnon is the unquestioned tone-setter in Colorado. Watching him fight -- twice! -- was as much for the Avalanche as it was for his own catharsis.

I asked one NHL player, who has never been MacKinnon's teammate, about his fights.

"If I'm on Colorado, I'm like, 'Wow, this guy is setting the tone,'" the player said. "He lost in the Olympics last year. [The Avs] lost in the playoffs. It looks like he's a man on a mission and willing to do whatever it takes. It's not like he's just doing it for dumb reasons."

Gallant likes a good superstar hockey fight. "It reminds you of the pure emotion some of these games carry. A guy like Tage Thompson of the Buffalo Sabres has had eight spirited bouts and he doesn't hold back. I imagine he'll have a few more as the years roll on," he said.

As far as stars that haven't fought yet, Gallant would like see what Oilers center Leon Draisaitl can do. His teammate, McDavid, hasn't had an NHL fight -- his last recorded bout on HockeyFights happened in 2014 while with the OHL Erie Otters. Macklin Celebrini, the consensus choice for the next face of the NHL, doesn't have an entry on his HockeyFights page while playing in his third NHL season. When he has his first fight, that clip probably goes supernova, given Mack's popularity.

OK, let's make that if he has his first fight. Or ever fights at all.

Teams by and large don't want their star players throwing punches. That goes for MacKinnon, too. "I think as the season goes on, you would see him do it less and less, just because it's very important to be healthy going into the playoffs," Johnson said.

Hockey fights are dangerous. Their infrequency in 2026 in comparison to previous decades should be lauded from a player safety perspective. As late as 2008-09, over 41% of all games featured a fight. That total was just 19% last season. I've written about factors in that decline before, with rules changes and the construction of team rosters as the main drivers.

While there's been a slight uptick in recent years, fighting remains infrequent in relation to how things used to be. I'd argue it's that infrequency that makes bouts like McBain vs. Frederic break through to general sports fans, or puts the spotlight on a player like MacKinnon when he fights. The NHL has gotten to a point where fighting remains part of the game but doesn't define the game, like back in the 1970s when the sport was a caricature of itself.

Many of the people I spoke with about this increase in fighting to start the season expect the trend to ebb by the end of the season. According to HockeyFights, the average number of fights per game has ranged between 0.23 and 0.25 for the last five seasons.

"I also just think it's cyclical, too. Some years are going to be up more than others," Johnson said. "But it is interesting to see that it's up this year."

Brady Tkachuk's return to Ottawa might not have been the most bilious homecoming in recent NHL history -- John Tavares' first game at Nassau Coliseum as a Maple Leafs holds that title belt, what with the rubber snakes tossed at him -- but it came close for sheer nastiness. The Ottawa fans chanted "eff" Brady and his podcast, as well as about him eating crayons; they brought signs mocking his fealty to brother Matthew and his playoff choke job; and, in the greatest tradition of these spiteful nights, they placed totems of Brady in arena urinals, from hockey cards to jersey nameplates.

Brady Tkachuk made the night even more special by leaning into the villainy. He scored Florida's lone goal to give them a 1-0 lead and temporarily mute the crowd. He had a Grinch-like grin when boos rained down during stoppages. By proclaiming in his podcast that he intended to donate any jerseys thrown on the ice to a local charity, he incepted Senators fans to throw several of them. What a night. Hockey!

LOSER: Jumbotron Tributes
What happened to our Revenge Game oasis? When Mitch Marner made his acrimonious return to Toronto as a Golden Knight, the fans parked their booing and chants during his Jumbotron tribute video, even cheering Marner before getting back to the spite soon afterwards.

But on Brady Tkachuk Night, the fans in Ottawa jeered through the entirety of the Senators' video tribute to their former captain, leading to surreal images such as Brady Tkachuk in a surgical mask visiting local children while the soundtrack is overwhelmed by hateful jeering. Again, hockey!

WINNER: Good lookin' Manny Malhotra
The fantasy sports site Rotogrinders did one of our favorite things recently: Creating an arbitrary sports ranking using a convoluted methodology. In this case, they ranked the most handsome NHL head coaches using a recipe of "Google's MediaPipe Face Mesh" and "468 facial reference points" and "four neoclassical and two landmark-based," which does sound better than "we threw a dart."

Based on this intricate system, Vancouver Canucks coach Manny Malhotra was ranked as the league's most handsome coach, followed closely by Vegas Golden Knights bench boss Ryan Craig. It's here we'll note that they're both in their first seasons as NHL head coaches, which explains a lot.

LOSER: Rick Bowness
The problem with putting your team on blast only a handful of games into the season is that a coach runs the risk of (a) not being able to effectively do it again and (b) potentially losing the team rather than lighting a fire under them.

Bowness has called out the Columbus Blue Jackets in public and in private, and the season is still spiraling. A mutual parting of ways seems like an inevitability if the Blue Jackets serve up a few more stinkers like that effort against Toronto this week.

WINNER: Vancouver Goldeneyes

In last week's column, we confessed our displeasure with the new PWHL Vegas jerseys. So it's only fair that we acknowledge the absolute perfection of these Vancouver Goldeneyes sweaters, built around a top tier hockey logo. A jersey worthy of the greatness that is KK Harvey.

LOSER: Cryptic marketing

We're very much looking forward to the Fanatics Hometown Remix jerseys that are coming soon. They were teased this week, as 31 teams released images of their new sweaters along with cryptic messages that needed to be descrambled -- like this Maple Leafs one that reads "It's Always About The Leafs."

I don't know ... I guess it works in theory. But it has very strong "Be Sure To Drink Your Ovaltine" energy.

FAVORITE ON-ICE MOMENT
Watching Connor McDavid, Leon Draisaitl, Zach Hyman and Evan Bouchard operate in a 4-on-3 power play in overtime is like having someone crank a Jack-in-the-Box that also plays your favorite song. Like, it's just a matter of time before it pops, as Bouchard did with the game winner against Minnesota. It's poetry.

It was also a reminder of a plank in my platform: That we scrap the overtime and shootout for dueling power plays, which is closer to what we watched in the previous 60 minutes. But that's a column for another time.

FAVORITE OFF-ICE MOMENT
We're officially giving Calgary Flames netminder Devin Cooley the "Ilya Bryzgalov Award For Goalie Who Should Absolutely Keep Talking."

After blessing the hockey world with "nothing matters, nobody cares, we're all going to die" as a calming mantra last season, Cooley went viral again for this interview in which he "felt nothing" in a recent game because his "conscious brain" is bad at playing goal in comparison to his "unconscious brain," which is apparently Vezina-worthy. He expanded on this on a Q&A with Sportsnet.

MUST-SEE GAMES

Anaheim Ducks at Philadelphia Flyers

Saturday, Oct. 24, 1 p.m. ET (NHL Network)

Almost-Flyer Leo Carlsson plays in Philadelphia for the first time since the Flyers made him the highest paid player in the NHL this season thanks to their offer sheet. On the undercard: The always interesting matchup between Flyers star Trevor Zegras and his former team. He scored two goals against Anaheim at home last season.

Minnesota Wild at Vancouver Canucks

Sunday, Oct. 25, 10 p.m. ET (ESPN+)

Now that we've seen how Ottawa fans have greeted the return of a former captain who was traded to play with his brother after informing his team he wasn't going to sign a new contract with them, Quinn Hughes plays in Vancouver for the first time following those exact circumstances. Well, save for the whole "playing with his brothers" thing. That comes later.

Boston Bruins at Carolina Hurricanes

Tuesday, Oct. 27, 7 p.m. ET (ESPN)

The Bruins were 7-2-1 in their first 10 games of the season, with the seventh-best offense and fourth best defense in the NHL during that span. The defending Stanley Cup champions will be a good measuring stick for coach Marco Sturm's Bruins, in their first meeting of the season.

PUCK HEADLINES
Dateline: Winnipeg
Let's talk Connor Hellebuyck.

The Winnipeg Jets goaltender's suspension ends this Friday. That's not an arbitrary end date. According to sources, Hellebuyck informed the Jets on Oct. 2 that he intended to end his training camp holdout and return to the team. They promptly used a cause in the CBA that gives teams power to suspend players who have "not received permission to be absent from training camp," with the suspension being at "a reasonable length."

I had one NHL agent wonder if Hellebuyck and his representation were aware of this CBA clause, given that he's lost upward of $900,000 and gained nothing insofar as leverage. At least Dylan Larkin had other fanbases desirously chanting his name.

Not a single source to whom I spoke this week believed that Hellebuyck would be traded before Friday, and that he'll end up collecting his paycheck while remaining back in Michigan, where ESPN's Emily Kaplan said he's been training.

It's been interesting to hear Winnipeg players creak the door open for a possible return to the team. Seeking reconciliation with estranged acquaintances is a basic human response -- some might say a character flaw -- and completely understandable when a player who has been in Winnipeg for 12 seasons decides to peace out.

Kyle Connor, a U.S. national teammate with Hellebuyck, has generally seemed devastated by the betrayal -- Hellebuyck was in his wedding party. Captain Adam Lowry has been more diplomatic, while acknowledging the extremely difficult healing that would have to happen should Hellebuyck return.

(Speaking of nuptials: Hellebuyck attended Lowry's wedding in July with a number of current teammates, with his desire to leave Winnipeg already widely reported by that point. I've sort of been obsessed with this. Did the Lowrys keep Hellebuyck at the same table seating for the reception or does a trade request put him in the back with the weird cousins instead of, like, next to Cole Perfetti?)

I've heard two opposing views on why a Hellebuyck deal hasn't happened yet. The first is that it's the player's fault: That Hellebuyck, who has a no-movement clause, wants to play for a Stanley Cup contender. Like, a sure thing team in the Carolina or Vegas or Florida sense. There are teams that have had talks with the Jets like Utah, Buffalo and Los Angeles, but they're not the level of contender Hellebuyck seeks. Again, that's from a few sources.

Other sources have indicated that it's GM Kevin Cheveldayoff holding up things here, as Hellebuyck would accept a move to places such as Buffalo or Los Angeles. But Cheveldayoff wants to hit a grand slam with his most tradable asset, and he's yet to be offered a deal that rises to that standard from a team for whom Hellebuyck is willing to play.

I tend to believe the latter scenario is the catalyst for this stalemate. I've heard the ask from the Jets is astronomical, and frankly that's justified given Hellebuyck's accomplishments. One last note: The NHLPA told me it wanted to see how it played out after his suspension ends before commenting on the Hellebuyck situation. I'd be surprised if there's a grievance filed in the near term, what with Hellebuyck getting paid not to play. There's precedent for that. But the question is how long that'll last.

Dateline: Detroit
As I reported this week, disgruntled former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin has now expanded his list of potential destinations to at least 10 teams.

We knew about the first three that he gave Detroit in the offseason: The Florida Panthers, Minnesota Wild and Vegas Golden Knights. The list is now expanded to the Carolina Hurricanes, Colorado Avalanche, Dallas Stars, New Jersey Devils, Tampa Bay Lightning, Utah Mammoth and Washington Capitals. Again, these are teams to whom Larkin would accept a trade. We don't know how deep talks have gone with any of them.

Toronto-based writer Jeff Veillette noted that Larkin's list includes nine of the top 10 teams in current Stanley Cup betting odds, with only the Edmonton Oilers excluded -- sources have told ESPN that Larkin doesn't want a trade to a Canadian team, despite the desires of Montreal fans.

One team I'm fascinated by on his list are the Capitals. They're off to a somewhat middling start. GM Chris Patrick has been very aggressive in adding talent to his lineup, from Pierre-Luc Dubois and Jacob Chychrun to Jordan Kyrou and Boone Jenner. He has a robust pipeline of young talent that could entice the Red Wings, plus an NHL center that can help them now in Dylan Strome, who is signed through next season ($5 million AAV) and has no trade protection.

Ultimately, I think the Capitals would rather upgrade their back end in their quest for a second Stanley Cup. But as always, they're one to keep an eye on.

stories.headline: UFC 333 preview and picks for featherweight, men's bantamweight titles
stories.summary: Check out the matchups and expert predictions for both championship fights at UFC 333 in Abu Dhabi.
stories.body:
How does a fighter know when to stop when they're fighting well?

It's a question that, unfortunately, rarely gets answered in MMA. For every athlete who retires from the sport on their own terms, there are at least two athletes being retired by the sport. It is rare for a fighter to go out on a win, and infinitely rare for a fighter to go out on top.

UFC featherweight champion Alexander Volkanovski (28-4) is starting to look that question in the face. Volkanovski will look to defend his title at UFC 333 on Saturday against 32-year-old Movsar Evloev (20-0) in Abu Dhabi, UAE. Volkanovski, 38, already is defying the rules of Father Time. In April 2025, he became the first fighter older than 35 to win a UFC championship belt in a weight class under 170 pounds. He defended that title in January against 31-year-old Diego Lopes.

In the past, Volkanovski has been dismissive, even comedic, of his age, starring in self-deprecating "Old Man Volk" skits on the internet. Ahead of UFC 333, however, he's been discussing age far more seriously, saying that any fight moving forward could be his last.

"There's a reason this is not often done," Volkanovski told ESPN. "I will bring up [my age], because I think it adds to the story. A lot of people are thinking about it. The young, undefeated guy -- facing the old, 38-year-old."

Evloev, of Russia, is one of the most proven title challengers in featherweight division history, with a perfect 10-0 record inside the Octagon, but he hasn't finished a single UFC opponent. He is a slight underdog against Volkanovski, according to DraftKings -- a credit to how good Volkanovski has looked, as well as lingering doubts on Evloev's ceiling.

Volkanovski, a two-time champion who suffered back-to-back knockout losses to Islam Makhachev and Ilia Topuria before regaining his title in 2025, told ESPN he believes he will actually look better than ever on Saturday, due to Evloev's style. The undefeated challenger is known primarily as a position-focused grappler, who might struggle to match Volkanovski's striking and scrambling ability.

"His style is a perfect matchup for me, I truly believe that," Volkanovski said. "I'm not delusional, saying I'm the best I've ever been at age 38. I'm not in my prime. But stylistically, I think you guys will be saying, 'I swear this is the best Volk we've ever seen.'"

Even if that is the case, odds say Volkanovski is tempting fate with every performance from this point forward. Male UFC fighters 38 and older have won 37% of their bouts all time, according to ESPN Research. Volkanovski has acknowledged as much and even proposed a "sendoff" title fight against 37-year-old lightweight champion Justin Gaethje next, after which they would both retire.

Volkanovski has stated he's taking it one fight at a time, but he is talking about retirement now, which shows he understands the decision is in front of him.

"One hundred percent, if I notice I'm slowing down or I'm taking more damage, [I'll retire]," Volkanovski said. "I said that before my last fight, too. A lot of people look at me saying that and say, 'Look how he's talking, his head isn't in it.' I'm just real and I'm honest. I said it before my last fight, and what happened? I went out there and made it look easy."

More storylines to watch

Dvalishvili looks to prove the last fight was an outlier
Merab Dvalishvili attempted to make history at the end of 2025, when he fought Petr Yan in his fourth men's bantamweight title defense of the calendar year. The feat has never been accomplished -- or even attempted -- and it proved to be too much as Dvalishvili lost a five-round decision. He later revealed he went into the bout with a significant knee injury and had a terrible camp. Dvalishvili (21-5) will try to recapture his title against Yan (20-5) in the UFC 333 co-main event.

Although he's admitted to tough circumstances around their last meeting, Dvalishvili has also said he doesn't regret pursuing UFC history and won't use those circumstances as an excuse, crediting Yan for the victory.

But the fighters' shared history has obviously raised the stakes for this Saturday. Dvalishvili and Yan have met twice, with Dvalishvili dominating their first meeting in March 2023. If Yan wins the trilogy, against a much fresher version of Dvalishvili than he saw in December, it could push Dvalishvili toward the back of the line for another title shot.

Not the last chance, but kind of the last chance
Not to put unnecessary pressure onto Aaron Pico's shoulders, but the truth is that any type of loss to Losene Keita -- a promising talent who is only 1-1 in the UFC -- would have heavy, long-lasting implications.

Pico, 30, has won 10 of his past 12 fights, but this is still a crossroads. He's been viewed as championship material since before his professional MMA debut, but has endured violent, memorable setbacks at various points in his career, including a spinning back elbow knockout loss to Lerone Murphy in his UFC debut 14 months ago. There is still massive potential in Pico, and he had an impressive bounce-back win against Patricio Pitbull in April, but he's in a risky position this weekend. He faces a dangerous but relatively unknown opponent in Keita after his original opponent, Arnold Allen, was forced off the card. Saturday's outcome will go a long way in determining how matchmakers and fans view him moving forward.

Coaches' questions and predictions for the title fights

Can Evloev significantly control Volkanovski on the ground?
Evloev is good everywhere, but Volkanovski has such an ability to game plan and show up in the big moments. Evloev is super big and strong. He has good standup, great transitions and ground control. But Volkanovski was able to get up after being taken down by Islam Makhachev. Are we just gonna forget that? Islam is now a welterweight. Volkanovski is so intelligent and so good at finding ways to exploit guys. His fight IQ is as good as anyone I've ever watched. He showed it against Lopes in their rematch in January. If Evloev cannot control Volk on the ground for long periods of time, Volkanovski will win a decision. And with the modern emphasis on damage when it comes to scoring, judges don't want to see you unsuccessfully try to hold someone down. Volkanovski by decision. -- Sayif Saud, Fortis MMA

Will age catch up to Volkanovski?
The biggest X factor is that unknown: At what point does Volkanovski's age slow him down? He's fighting one of the purest wrestlers/grapplers in the UFC in Evloev. I could see Evloev trying to prove he can stand with Volkanovski at times and win over the UFC, but I don't think that would be his smartest decision. Personally, I believe that "Old Man Volk" still has it. He's proven time and again he's going to win those key wrestling scrambles, and I believe he'll end up catching Movsar. It will be a grinder of a fight, but Volkanovski's experience being in there with bigger, stronger guys like Islam will pay off. Volkanovski by TKO. -- John Wood, Syndicate MMA

Can Dvavishvili hurt Yan with his hands?
We know that Yan has the physicality to compete with Merab's wrestling. He didn't avoid the takedown in their last fight -- he actually got more takedowns than Merab. That's a fact. And Yan on the feet is so dangerous, you have to give his standup the edge. If he comes in in great shape and can counter-wrestle and have the same physicality he did in December, he can win. The biggest technical question is whether Merab can create enough offense to get inside and hurt Yan with his hands. If the wrestling gets shut down, can he create offense? If Merab can hurt Yan on the feet, that changes the whole fight and throws it in favor of Merab. I've got Yan winning by a slight edge. -- Saud

Who will control the resets?
Yan needs to control the range, punish Merab's entries and continually invest in the body. He needs to establish the center and force Merab to initiate his wrestling from a distance, and intersect those entries with straight punches, body shots and uppercuts. I'd like to see him keep that lead arm frame, to establish his underhooks right away with his wrestling defense. He doesn't need to eliminate the takedown attempt, but he does need to make Merab pay for every failed attempt. Merab, meanwhile, has to weaponize pace, create chaos and disrupt Yan's comfort. He has to chain together multiple takedown attempts, so that even failed attempts affect Yan's rhythm. Who will control the resets? Merab thrives when one attack becomes three or four; Yan thrives when he's able to reset and return to technical striking. I lean Yan by decision again. --Eric Nicksick, Xtreme Couture

stories.headline: St. Louis GK Bürki stretchered off after collision in Open Cup final
stories.summary: St. Louis goalkeeper Roman Bürki was taken to the hospital after taking a knock to the head during the U.S. Open Cup final against the Columbus Crew.
stories.body:
St. Louis City goalkeeper Roman Bürki was taken to the hospital after taking a knock to the head in a collision during his team's U.S. Open Cup final win over the Columbus Crew on Wednesday night.

In an attempt to make a save in the 70th minute, Bürki took a knee to the head from Crew winger Anass Zaroury. He remained on the ground to receive medical attention before being stretchered off the field.

Bürki was able to wave to supporters as he was taken away from the pitch. St. Louis confirmed to ESPN that Bürki was conscious and moving all extremities on his way to the hospital.

"He is currently alert and in good spirits. The club's medical staff will continue to monitor his condition and the team will provide additional updates as they become available," the club later said in a statement on X.

The score was tied 0-0 at the time of the injury, but St. Louis went on to win the game in a shootout after Burki's backup Ben Lundt made a save to help his team beat the Crew 5-3 on spot kicks.

The win earned St. Louis, which began play in MLS in 2023, its first trophy in club history.

St. Louis City captain Bürki had 43 touches and three crucial saves before the injury. He played an integral role in maintaining the 0-0 draw before being replaced by Lundt after the head injury.

Bürki, who joined St. Louis from Borussia Dortmund in 2022, stopped a corner kick from Brais Méndez that appeared to be goalbound and a flurry of other shots just before sustaining his injury.

Eleven minutes of injury time was added due to Bürki's injury, but neither team scored before the end of regulation despite Columbus outshooting St. Louis 16-3, so the game went to extra time and penalties.

stories.headline: Consensus top AFL draft prospect Dougie Cochrane already in rare air
stories.summary: Missing significant chunks of football hasn't stopped Port Adelaide NGA star Dougie Cochrane from firming as the top prospect in this year's AFL draft.
stories.body:
It's rare for a player to be the consensus no. 1 rated prospect in their draft. From coaches to recruiters and a myriad of draft evaluators, Dougie Cochrane stands atop 2026's crop. For him to do so after playing just four games in his top-age campaign puts the Port Adelaide NGA gun in rare air.

The starring junior missed both years of his u18 national championships through injury, and this year only returned to the field in the final month of the season. But what he produced at league level last season and amongst his peers at the u16s national championships in 2024 is not easily forgotten.

Clearly a class above at the national championships three years ago, Cochrane put all of his skill and athleticism on show. He was a distributor out of defence, won aerial duels around the ground and was the focal point of the SA forward line in a showing of his unique versatility.

From there he made his league debut for Central Districts as a 17-year-old, kicking four goals including an outrageous snap on his left foot from the pocket after crumbing a forward 50 contest. From his first game he was already the best player on the ground.

Speaking to ESPN ahead of the draft combine Cochrane was a bit flat. It wasn't because he'd missed his top-age season, he knew he wasn't going to be testing, and he knew most clubs wouldn't bother booking an interview given his ties to Port Adelaide. But there was one thing that really got to him.

"They measured me at 194-and-a-half centimetres," he tells ESPN with a grin. "They took a centimetre off me, but we'll round that up."

At six-foot-four (we'll round it up too) he's widely considered the next elite key forward prospect to come through the AFL Draft. Only he doesn't necessarily see it that way.

"I want to be a midfielder when I'm older, that's what I'm striving towards. "For right now I'm pretty happy forward, if not back. I'm happy wherever the team needs, whatever the team needs.

"I'm pretty skinny right now, I'm not as muscly as the Patty Cripps's of the world, the Bonts of the world. I want to focus on my midfield craft and get that experience."

Cochrane missed a significant chunk of his bottom-age year with a hamstring and over the off-season underwent knee surgery to address patella tendinitis. He didn't play for 11 straight months from the end of 2025 to July 2026.

Watching from the sidelines frustrated him but he knew it was all out of an abundance of caution.

"I started playing league at Centrals last year, I sort of started feeling [knee pain] a little bit. I thought nothing of it, just thought it was a bit of growing pain. It got worse and worse by the time I started doing pre-season... when you take off and do your powerful stuff it flares up.

"They did a clean out of it... I had the surgery, and I walked out of the surgery. It was two little key holes."

Cochrane sat down with ESPN as Port Adelaide list manager Jason Cripps all but confirmed on Trade Radio Essendon would be bidding on the gun academy prospect at pick one in the 2026 AFL Draft.

He's the son of Port Adelaide and North Melbourne midfielder Stuart Cochrane, and grew up supporting the Power after his dad's playing career finished up. His brother Tom was on the list during formative years and the club is set up to match his bid wherever it lands.

"Dad's been my idol growing up. Looking up to him, I obviously didn't get to see him play but he's been enormous."

Asked if it would mean more being that first selection on November 19, Cochrane's humble nature shines through.

"I loved watching the draft growing up, seeing those high picks. The pick doesn't really matter, does it? There have been a lot of picks over times where the number one picks haven't gone as well as they should've. I just want to end up at an AFL club - wherever that is I don't mind - but I just want to play footy," he says.

"Growing up and supporting Port all my life, it would be special playing for them. But whatever happens happens and I'm just gonna let that decide itself."

stories.headline: NRL transfer whispers: Bulldogs closing in on Skelton return; Panthers lock in Patea
stories.summary: The NRL season may be over, but the player market is already heating up ahead of November 1. Isaac Issa has news from the Dragons on some key outside backs
stories.body:
The NRL season may be over, but the player market is already heating up ahead of November 1, with clubs beginning to shape their rosters for 2027 and beyond.

From player movement to changes behind the scenes, ESPN NRL Insider Isaac Issa has the latest whispers from around the competition.

Cowboys open to keeping Taumalolo

North Queensland are open to retaining Jason Taumalolo beyond 2027, with the veteran forward's assessment of how his body is holding up set to guide the next step.

ESPN understands the Cowboys will take their lead from Taumalolo as he weighs up his playing future, reflecting his standing as a club legend.

Taumalolo is contracted until the end of next season and becomes eligible to negotiate with rival clubs for 2028 onwards from November 1.

Panthers lock in Patea
Penrith have secured Tua Patea until the end of 2029, with the youngster signing an extension that includes a pathway from a development contract into the club's top 30.

Patea capped off the 2026 season with a hat-trick in the Panthers' Jersey Flegg Grand Final victory, having started the year with an NRL training block.

The new deal will see him join Penrith's full-time NRL squad as he works towards a first-grade debut.

Bulldogs closing in on Skelton return

Jeral Skelton is closing in on a return to Canterbury following his departure from the Wests Tigers.

ESPN understands the Bulldogs are in advanced discussions to bring the outside back to the club for the 2027 season.

An agreement is understood to be close, although the deal has yet to be finalised.

Multiple NRL sides eye Knights forward

A Sydney club and a Queensland-based club are monitoring Newcastle forward Mat Croker ahead of November 1.

ESPN understands the two clubs have shown interest in the 27-year-old, who is approaching the final year of his Knights contract and can negotiate with rivals for 2028 onwards from next month.

Rivals keeping tabs on Dragons' Tu

Multiple clubs are monitoring St George Illawarra outside back Setu Tu, with the Dragons yet to begin talks over a contract extension.

Tu is contracted until the end of 2027 and is expected to test the open market from November 1, when rival clubs can negotiate a deal for 2028 and beyond.

The former Warriors outside back joined the Dragons on a development contract this season and is set to move into the club's top 30 squad in 2027.

His ability to cover multiple positions across the backline adds to his appeal as clubs assess their recruitment options.

Rivals monitor Patea as open market looms
Penrith young gun Luron Patea is expected to test the open market from November 1, with multiple clubs keeping tabs on the promising prop.

Patea is contracted until the end of 2027, but the Panthers are yet to begin talks over an extension, leaving rival clubs poised to explore a deal for 2028 and beyond.

Penrith have not granted Patea permission to negotiate with other clubs before November 1.

The Panthers junior made his NRL debut in 2024 and has shown promise during his first-grade opportunities, providing another emerging option in Penrith's forward pack.

He is among several Panthers players approaching the final year of their contracts, with veteran prop Moses Leota also unsigned beyond 2027.

Roosters eye Dockar-Clay reunion
The Roosters have shown interest in a potential return for Zach Dockar-Clay as they explore options to bolster their hooking and utility depth.

ESPN understands the 31-year-old has emerged as an option following his departure from Manly, with discussions remaining at an early stage.

Dockar-Clay spent the 2024 and 2025 seasons with the Roosters before joining the Sea Eagles on a one-year deal for 2026.

Manly confirmed his departure last month after a season in which he claimed the club's NSW Cup best-and-fairest award.

Bostock brushes Dragons links

Dolphins star Jack Bostock has dismissed recent links between himself and the Dragons, admitting this isn't the first time he'd been floated for a club switch.

"I've been linked to a few a clubs," Bostock admitted.

"I don't know about [the Dragons links]."

He said that while he "obviously sees it in the media," his sole focus is the Kangaroos.

Sloan's Dragons stay still a possibility

Tyrell Sloan could yet remain at St George Illawarra next season, with discussions ongoing over a potential stay despite his planned move to Castleford.

There is interest in keeping Sloan at the Dragons, but several hurdles remain before that can become a reality.

Roster space and salary cap room would need to be worked through, while any arrangement would also require Castleford to agree to release him.

Sloan previously admitted he would "love to" remain in the NRL when speaking to Channel Nine in August, after his Castleford deal had been announced.

No agreement has been reached and a stay is far from guaranteed.

stories.headline: The Seahawks prepare to face former teammate Kenneth Walker III while Zack Charbonnet could return
stories.summary: As the Seahawks prepare to face former teammate Kenneth Walker III, they may be getting some help with their own running game.
stories.body:
As the Seahawks prepare to face former teammate Kenneth Walker III, they may be getting some help with their own running game.


Seahawks running back Zack Charbonnet may play for the first time this season Sunday when Seattle hosts the undefeated Kansas City Chiefs. He participated in a full practice Wednesday and was placed on the active roster Thursday.


His return couldn't come at a better time for the Seahawks, who are coming off a 17-14 loss to the Denver Broncos last Thursday night. It was the third loss this season for the defending Super Bowl champions.


The Seahawks' run game has struggled for much of the season and they could use Charbonnet, who tore his ACL in January and spent the first six games of the season on the physically unable to perform list.


"There is a possibility that you can see him on Sunday in some capacity," Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald said this week.


Seattle is ranked 18th in the league with an average of 107.2 total yards on the ground this season. They have five rushing touchdowns. Rookie Jadarian Price, who was expected to help, is out with a chest/shoulder injury.


Charbonnet rushed for 730 yards and 12 touchdowns for the Seahawks last season before he was injured.


Of course, one of the reasons why Seattle's run game has dipped this season is the loss of Walker, their Super Bowl MVP who went to the Chiefs as a free agent in the offseason


"But I think there’s mixed emotions. We’re happy for him, but also, we’re trying to figure out ways to stop this guy, too," Macdonald said.


Walker rushed for 128 yards and two touchdowns in Kansas City's 22-6 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday. It was the fourth game he's topped 100 yards rushing this season. Walker is averaging a league-leading 133 yards rushing per game and has run for eight touchdowns so far.


Walker became the Seahawks' top back after Charbonnet was injured, and ran for 135 yards in the Super Bowl against the Patriots to earn MVP honors.


Chiefs coach Andy Reid expects Walker to treat his return to Seattle like he does every game.


“I think the boys there will try to get after him a little bit. But he’s a pretty level-headed guy. The way he plays, you’re going to get a good rep when he gets the ball in his hands,” Reid said. "He kind of has one speed: He’s coming at you. It doesn’t matter who he’s playing or where he’s playing.”

stories.headline: World Series preview: Surprising Rays-Brewers showdown to open with Jacob Misiorowski's record heat
stories.summary: — The Miz will try to whiz his famous fastball by batters on baseball's biggest stage, opening a new-look World Series between teams guaranteed to produce a first-time champion.
stories.body:
MILWAUKEE -- — The Miz will try to whiz his famous fastball by batters on baseball's biggest stage, opening a new-look World Series between teams guaranteed to produce a first-time champion.


Jacob Misiorowski brings his record-setting heat to the mound for the Milwaukee Brewers on Friday night when he throws the first pitch of the best-of-seven championship against the Tampa Bay Rays, a matchup of modest-money marvels who bumped off glamorous rivals with a throwback base-to-base style.


“Forrest Gump, everyone,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said Thursday, introducing his ace to the assembled media.


“I'm still fresh to this and have no idea what the hell is going on,” Misiorowski said a few minutes later.


Few predicted this pairing of pennant winners when the season opened March 25. The first World Series with robot umpires is the first since 1980 between teams seeking their first championship and also could be the first with a 104 mph pitch — thanks to Misiorowski — and the first to be played totally indoors.


"I’m excited to see two great teams that play the game a little differently than maybe it’s been played the last decade or so,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said.


Milwaukee is in the Series for the second time after a 44-year absence — an appropriate number given that it was the jersey of the Cream City's most famous baseball player, Hank Aaron, who became a star with the Milwaukee Braves in the 1950s and ended his career with the expansion Brewers in the 1970s.


Both teams fell short in previous Series trips, the Brewers losing to St. Louis in 1982 and the Rays to Philadelphia in 2008 and to the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2020. Not since the Phillies beat Kansas City in 1980 have two teams met seeking their first title. The time before that was in 1920.


Misiorowski is likely to set a World Series velocity record
Misiorowski, a 24-year-old right-hander in his first full major league season, is a starting pitcher like no other. He threw 1,115 pitches of 100 mph or higher this year — shattering the old high of 673 since tracking began in 2008, by Jordan Hicks in 2018.


His fastest pitch was 105.5 mph to the Chicago Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong on June 27, and he appears likely to break the 101.1 mph record for a Series starter by the New York Mets' Noah Syndergaard in 2015 and possibly the overall Series high of 103.2 mph by Cubs reliever Aroldis Chapman to Cleveland's Coco Crisp in Game 2 of 2016.


Misiorowski didn't finish the fifth inning in either of his first two postseason starts this year. Batters have swung at 94 of his 182 postseason pitches and fouled off 51 — 28% of pitches and 54% of swings.


“He hasn’t been as crisp,” Murphy said. “They’re obviously looking at an area. They’re trying to exploit everything. He’s exposed, like all these guys get at some point.”


The Brewers and Rays have throwback offenses
In an age where power bats usually rule, Milwaukee scored a major league-low 32.1% of its runs on homers and Tampa Bay was second-lowest at 34.4%, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.


“It's cool that you don't have to be that team to hit 170 home runs a game or whatever,” Misiorowski said. “You can win a baseball game so many different ways.”


Rays batters had the fewest strikeouts among the 30 teams and Tampa Bay’s 45 sacrifice bunts were the most among American League teams since 2015.


“I was a little discouraged for the last 10 or 15 years in the way the game had gone as far as relying on the home run, not worrying about strikeouts,” said Hall of Famer Robin Yount, a star of the '82 Brewers. “The game today looks like they’re starting to really focus on playing baseball again.”


After back-to-back Dodgers titles, MLB will have a small-payroll champion
This marks the first time since 1991 that both Series teams are in the bottom half of payrolls: the Brewers were 19th as of Aug. 31 and the Rays 25th. Milwaukee, MLB's smallest market, could become the first small-market champion since Kansas City in 2015. The Rays rank 15th in market size.


To reach the Series, the Brewers swept the deep-pocketed, two-time champion Dodgers in the NL Championship Series and the Rays swept the New York Yankees in an AL Division Series.


The highest-paid player in the Series, Brewers outfielder Christian Yelich, was 44th overall in the majors on opening day. Yandy Díaz, who earns most among the Rays, ranked 154th.


Robot umps are changing games
Batters have succeeded on 63% of challenges during the postseason in the first year of the Automated Ball-Strike System, winning 40 of 63 appeals to the robot umps. That is up from 49% during the regular season.


Catchers' 58% success rate in the playoffs (58 of 99) is down a tick from 59% during the regular season and pitchers are 1 for 1 — Tampa Bay’s Griffin Jax made the only challenge. The 60% overall rate is up from 54% in the regular season.


Tampa Bay's batters have yet to make a postseason challenge. Milwaukee's have won 4 of 7, including a perfect 2 for 2 by Jake Bauers.


Brewers catcher William Contreras has won 60% (12 of 20) and Rays catcher Liam Hicks 67% (8 of 12).


Rest vs rust: Extra time off hasn't been helpful in recent years
Milwaukee will have had seven days off going into the opener.


While teams with less rest are 15-15 in the Series since Wild Card Era started in 1995, they are 12-4 since 2009.


Both teams are happy at home
Milwaukee and Tampa Bay tied for the best home record this year at 55-26.


Forced from Tropicana Field for 2025 after damage from Hurricane Milton, the Rays played across the bay at the Yankees’ spring training stadium in St. Petersburg, Florida, and then returned to the refurbished Trop for 2026.
